opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the toy model is really simple, and that's kind of the point. Imagine that for some task the model has to get a sequence of, say, L tokens all correct for the answer to count, which is what exact match or similar all-or-nothing metrics are doing. And suppose, just as a simplification, that the per-token probability of being correct is p, and the tokens are roughly independent. Then the probability of getting the whole thing right is p to the L.

Now think about what happens as you scale the model. Empirically, per-token quantities like cross-entropy loss improve smoothly and predictably with scale. That's the whole scaling-laws story. So p creeps up smoothly, maybe from 0.8 to 0.85 to 0.9 and so on. But when you raise that to the power L, with L being, say, five or ten or more, the curve becomes this very nonlinear thing. It sits near zero for a long stretch, and then fairly abruptly shoots up toward one. If you plot that on a log-scale x-axis of parameters or compute, which is how everyone plots these things, it looks like a sharp, unpredictable jump, a phase transition.

So the inference is that the apparent sharpness doesn't have to come from anything fundamentally discontinuous happening inside the model. It can be produced entirely by the researcher's choice of metric. The underlying capability is improving smoothly, and a nonlinear or discontinuous scoring function, such as exact match or multiple-choice grade, makes it look emergent.

That leads to a few testable predictions, which is what we actually went and checked. First, if you take the same model outputs and swap in a continuous or linear metric, like token edit distance or Brier score instead of accuracy, the sharp transition should mostly go away and you should see smooth, predictable improvement. And we largely saw that. Second, resolution matters. If you don't evaluate on enough test examples, you can't distinguish tiny nonzero accuracies from zero, so everything looks flat at zero and then suddenly isn't. With a big enough test set you can see the small models are actually doing slightly better than zero, on a smooth trajectory. Third, and I think this is the most convincing piece, you can go the other way: take a setting where nobody claims emergence, like simple vision models, and by choosing a harsh enough metric you can manufacture something that looks just like an emergent ability.

I want to be careful about what we're not claiming. We're not saying large models can't have qualitatively new capabilities, or that nothing interesting happens with scale. And the independence assumption is obviously a simplification. Real token errors are correlated. The claim is narrower: many of the reported emergent abilities, the sharp unpredictable ones, are well explained by how we measure, not necessarily by a change in the model's behavior. Practically, that's actually good news. If capability gains are smoother than they looked, they're more predictable, which matters a lot for forecasting and for safety planning.

r001.rationale: The response explains that whole-sequence accuracy follows p^L and describes how that curve produces an apparently abrupt jump as per-token accuracy improves, linking the apparent transition to p and sequence length.

r002.rationale: It states that small models have accuracy slightly above zero on a smooth trajectory, consistent with a positive per-token correctness probability yielding a nonzero chance of getting the full sequence right.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the simple model is really just this: imagine a model has some per-token probability of getting a token right, and that probability improves smoothly with scale. Nothing dramatic happens there, it's just a nice, gradual curve. But now suppose your task requires getting, say, five tokens all correct, or ten, or a hundred. Then the probability of the whole thing being correct is roughly that per-token probability raised to the power of the sequence length.

What that does is take a smooth, boring curve and turn it into something that looks very sharp. When the per-token accuracy is, I don't know, 0.9, and you need a hundred tokens correct, you're essentially at zero. And as that per-token accuracy creeps up toward 0.99, 0.999, suddenly the task-level accuracy shoots up. So from the outside it looks like the model "couldn't do it, couldn't do it, and then suddenly could," which is exactly the thing people call emergence or a phase transition.

The inference we draw from that is that a lot of apparent phase transitions are an artifact of the metric, not evidence of something qualitatively new happening inside the model. The underlying capability was improving the whole time. The discontinuity comes from the fact that the metric is a nonlinear, and particularly a very unforgiving, function of the underlying smooth quantity. Exact-match accuracy on long outputs is the extreme version of that, but multiple choice accuracy with a threshold has the same flavor.

And the flip side, which I think is actually the more useful takeaway, is that if you choose a metric that's linear in the thing that's actually improving, like per-token log likelihood or some kind of partial credit, the jump goes away. You see the same models, the same scaling, and it looks smooth and predictable. That matters a lot if you care about forecasting what models will be able to do, because a smooth curve is something you can extrapolate, and a cliff is not.

So I'd put it this way: the simple model doesn't rule out that genuinely surprising capabilities could show up. It just says the burden of proof should be higher. Before you say "this is emergent," you should check whether a smoother metric on the same task tells a boring story, and quite often it does.

r001.rationale: It explains that raising smoothly improving per-token accuracy to the sequence length produces a sharp task-level rise, illustrating how the model accounts for apparent emergence.

r002.rationale: It gives whole-sequence correctness as roughly per-token accuracy raised to sequence length; for a positive per-token probability, that remains positive even when it is described as “essentially at zero.”

astra-6.text:
The main takeaway is that an apparent phase transition doesn’t necessarily mean there’s a sudden change in the underlying capability. Suppose the probability of getting each token right improves smoothly. If we assume those probabilities are independent, then the probability of getting an entire sequence right is their product. For a long sequence, that probability can remain very small and then rise quite sharply, even though the token-level probabilities are changing smoothly.

So if your metric is whether the whole answer is exactly correct, you might see what looks like a capability suddenly emerging. If you instead measure how many tokens are correct, you could see gradual progress. That doesn’t establish that every observed phase transition is a measurement effect. It shows that the shape of the curve alone isn’t enough to conclude that something fundamentally discontinuous happened inside the model.

r001.rationale: The response says the product probability can rise sharply and create an apparent emergence, but it does not state that the model predicts where the phase transition occurs.

r002.rationale: It says exact-sequence success can remain very small, but does not clearly state that the probability is nonzero in the low-performance region when each token has positive correctness probability.

sol-6.1.text:
The main takeaway is that an apparent phase transition doesn’t necessarily imply a sudden change in the underlying capability. Imagine that the probability of getting each token right improves smoothly. If your metric requires the entire answer to be correct, and we assume the tokens are independent, then the probability of success is the product of those token probabilities. For a long enough answer, that can stay very small and then rise sharply, even though each token probability is changing smoothly.

So you can see something that looks like an emergent ability just from the way you measure performance. That doesn’t rule out real phase transitions, but it means the sharp curve alone isn’t enough evidence. You need to look at what’s happening underneath the aggregate metric.

r001.rationale: The response explains that multiplying smoothly improving token probabilities can create a sharp rise in whole-answer success, but it does not state that the model predicts where the apparent phase transition occurs.
